item.title: Your AI Agents Need A Chief Operating Officer, Too
item.description:
By Rick Folgmann

A landlord in California has 21 days after a resident moves out to return the security deposit or send an itemized list of deductions. Miss it in bad faith, and the penalty can reach twice the deposit. That deadline doesn’t care whether the letter was supposed to come from a person or a piece of software. Either way, someone will answer for it.

I think about this a lot. At my company, Get Covered , we now run 16 AI agents across more than 3 million rental units. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to.

Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years.

Gartner , meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.

Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review.

Here is what has worked for us, and what I would advise any decision-maker to focus on when it comes to scaling.

Start with work that already has a rulebook

The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement.

Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified.

Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls.

McKinsey ‘s most recent State of AI research found that the small group of companies seeing significant bottom-line returns from AI, about 6% of respondents, were nearly 3x as likely to have fundamentally redesigned their workflows.

In my experience, that redesign starts with writing the rule down. If a new hire couldn’t follow your description of a decision on the person’s first day, an agent won’t follow it either.

Set autonomy by workflow

Tech execs I speak with often ask whether an AI system is autonomous, as if that were a fixed property of the product. In practice, the same agent should run with different levels of freedom depending on what it touches.

At Get Covered, we configure each agent on different levels. For instance, a reminder to a vendor whose certificate expires next month can go out automatically. A response to a resident who has requested an emotional support animal never does.

A useful exercise for any leadership team is to list every workflow an agent will touch and ask one question about each: If this action is wrong, how long until we find out, and what will it have cost by then? Quick detection and low cost earn an agent more room.

Give every agent an owner with a name

Earlier in my career I learned that every automated credit decision eventually had to be explained to a customer, a regulator, or both. The model did it was never an acceptable answer.

That still holds, except agents now act more often and across more systems than any underwriting model did.

So every agent at our company has a person ultimately responsible, the same way a team or a budget does. That person reviews its error log, decides when to widen or narrow its autonomy, and answers for it.

Ownership also heads off a quieter problem. When several teams launch agents independently, nobody sees where those agents contradict one other.

Where the constraint actually sits

In today’s marketplace, it’s inevitable that the models will keep improving. A company’s clarity about who decides what will not improve on its own. Gartner’s cancellation forecast reflects that: Most agent projects that fail will do so because nobody defined the value or controlled the risk, and both of those are management problems.

For decision-makers heading into 2027, my advice is to treat each agent the way you would treat a new employee in a regulated role. Write down its rules, limit its scope, and assign it a manager who checks its work and discusses its performance.

Companies that do this will be able to give agents more responsibility over time, because they will have the evidence to justify it. Businesses that skip it will spend 2027 explaining why their software did something nobody approved.

Rick Folgmann is chief operating officer at Get Covered , an insurance technology company that provides cost-effective property coverage with just a few clicks. He has more than 25 years of executive leadership experience in the financial and insurance industries.

item.title: Some Observations About Anthropic’s IPO Filing
item.description:
In an S-1 filing today preceding what could be the largest IPO ever , Anthropic laid out extensive new details about its earnings, growth, key stakeholders and the risks it faces going forward.

Clocking in at 335 pages, the document wasn’t exactly light reading. However, after a preliminary once-over, we highlight a few of the more intriguing disclosures below:

Revenue growth is unusually rapid

For the first half of this year, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion. That’s up 14x from the same period in 2025.

Things aren’t slowing either. While the S-1 doesn’t forecast the second half of this year, Reuters has reported that Anthropic could reach a $110 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end, citing analysts who met with company executives.

But losses persist

Anthropic also posted a $693 million operating income loss for the first half of 2026, down about two-thirds from last year. Its net loss for this year’s first half was $80 billion, of which about 90% stemmed from what it called a “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE s.”

Founders hold similar stakes

Each of Anthropic’s seven founders holds between 230,000 and 246,000 shares of Class A stock, per the S-1. This kind of egalitarianism seems unusual given that startup prospectuses usually show a founding CEO with a much larger relative stake compared to co-founders.

The company’s co-founders include Dario Amodei , Daniela Amodei , Tom Brown , Jack Clark , Jared Kaplan , Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah .

Anthropic’s risk factors take up 93 pages of its IPO filing

So, is investing in Anthropic a risky bet?

Anthropic certainly seems to think so. The company’s IPO prospectus contains a staggering 93 pages of risk factors. They start at page 27 and end on page 120.

Some are pretty mundane. For instance, the company is concerned that slower revenue growth could potentially constrain its ability to fund frontier AI development and attract and retain top talent. Having incurred significant debt to date, it’s worried about the ability to keep servicing those obligations while still covering operating costs.

But more unusual risks, like rogue AI agents, are in there too. In one section, Antrophic notes that “future models are expected to demonstrate capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons.”

item.title: When Traction Becomes Personal Exposure: What The Joonko Guilty Plea Means For Founders
item.description:
By Kyle Jeziorski

Ilit Raz , founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko , raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders.

Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison.

Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court.

Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research . The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction.

Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud

The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability.

Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred:

  • LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.”
  • Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth.
  • Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue.
  • Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own.

Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest?

Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims.

An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout.

Where D&O coverage may stop

Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends.

As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage.

Three policy provisions deserve attention:

  • The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions.
  • Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted.
  • Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances.

D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced.

Practical steps for founders before presenting metrics

Before sharing a pitch deck, create an easily accessible guide for your team that spells out your math. Specify what counts as a paying customer, how pilots and LOIs are classified, and how recurring revenue and churn are calculated. Use those definitions consistently.

Team with finance and legal advisers to connect material claims to supporting records, including executed contracts, invoices, accounting data and customer-status reports. Keep projections separate from current results, and document the assumptions behind the forecasts.

Don’t confuse ARR with cash collected; they do not belong in the same category. Show clearly how the company calculates recurring revenue and distinguishes it from one-time fees, pipeline opportunities and contracted commitments that haven’t gone live yet. Remember that ARR and contracted ARR are distinct metrics, not to be used interchangeably.

Lastly, date the figures and update material changes before investors rely on them for decision-making. If the team can’t explain how they calculate a number or substantiate a customer claim, resolve the discrepancy before presenting your deck.

Investors might buy into your vision, but regulators will look at your math.

Kyle Jeziorski is the market-facing and client leader at Founder Shield, the innovation arm of The Baldwin Group , with eight years invested in the boutique broker and more than a decade in the insurance industry. Before Founder Shield, he worked at Marsh on the FINPRO team focusing on management liability in the large private and public space. A graduate of Saint Joseph’s University ’s risk management and insurance program, Jeziorski has focused his entire career helping clients navigate through an ever-changing risk environment.

item.title: California Startups Have Raised More So Far In 2026 Than The Entire US Ever Has In A Single Year
item.description:
California companies have scooped up more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding this year. That, per Crunchbase data, is an apparent record share.

But that’s not all. As investment hit unprecedented levels in 2026, Golden State companies alone raised more than all U.S. startups in any prior year on record. Most of that stems from a handful of megarounds for San Francisco-based AI pioneers.

And keep in mind: This year still has a couple months left. Yet California companies have already pulled in an unparalleled $385 billion in seed- through growth-stage rounds. That’s more than double last year’s tally.

California’s share of U.S. startup funding also has been trending higher for the past three years. Much of this is due to San Francisco AI unicorns, but we’re also seeing strength in the broader Silicon Valley region as well as Southern California.

Where the money went

Flabbergasting financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic account for more than half of this year’s California statewide tally. But even without those, California companies

1 still secured a disproportionate share of the largest U.S. equity funding rounds.

To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 next-largest California funding rounds this year.

Some of these are familiar names and involve fairly mature companies. For instance Waymo , which launched inside Google in 2009 and spun out as an independent company 10 years ago, picked up $16 billion in February.

Another old-timer is Databricks , which picked up $5 billion in August. It’s now 13 years old and has raised over $30 billion in debt and equity funding to date.

Still, we’re also seeing younger companies secure megarounds. Prometheus , the physical AI startup co-founded and led by Jeff Bezos and launched last year, pulled in $12 billion in new funding this spring. And AI model startup Safe Superintelligence landed $5 billion in a Nvidia -led round this summer.

Early-stage funding

That brings us to our next point. California’s startup funding windfall isn’t only about late-stage and pre-IPO companies bagging enormous rounds. Early- and seed-stage companies are also attracting big checks from investors.

Per Crunchbase data, California companies have secured nearly $62 billion in seed- and early-stage financings so far in 2026. That’s roughly 57% of all U.S. funding at these stages.

It’s also far above prior year tallies, as charted below, and appears to be a record funding level.

Don’t bet against California

If there’s a lesson to be learned in these numbers, it’s one that savvy startup investors ought to have learned a long time ago: Don’t bet against California.

Whatever the year, whatever the technology cycle, California, and Silicon Valley in particular, have a knack for being home to the leading companies of the era.

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here .

It was another interesting week for AI-related startup funding, with a number of large rounds and quirky companies. The largest financings went to Tenstorrent , a developer of AI processors and systems, and AI lab Flapping Airplanes . The quirkiest round, meanwhile, was undoubtedly a $200 million financing for Warhound , which wants to breed elite military dogs.

A number of big rounds in areas including biotech, space tech and physical AI rounded out the list.

item.title: Protecting Trade Secrets In The Age Of AI
item.description:
By Seth Kugler

If you only have six months of experience in an industry, you usually aren’t equipped to poach your employer’s clients and start a competing business. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you.

That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss , attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services.

AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI.

Key lessons for founders

AI contamination cannot be undone

The defense in this case argued that because their client placed the stolen documents in a “quarantine folder” and no clients had been poached yet, no harm had been done.

The court appropriately recognized that the “quarantine folder” was grossly insufficient, granting our temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction while recognizing the competing AI agent as an “existential threat.”

An agreement not to touch just the stolen documents themselves is essentially irrelevant once AI gets involved: If a trade secret is used to develop a machine learning model or used to train an AI agent with recursive capabilities, it contaminates the model and the impact can be difficult to undo. Even if raw source files are completely scrubbed of any direct evidence of stolen materials, defendants will struggle to prove to courts that the AI isn’t operating a certain way precisely because it once had access to that proprietary information.

Personal devices can pose big risks

While trade secret misappropriation has typically been malicious, AI now also creates significant risks of inadvertent violations. Startups frequently scale with employees working on personal devices under standard Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements. Running desktop AI agents on these devices can pose a serious risk.

Unlike standard web interfaces, a desktop AI agent can scan files, create folders and ingest directory paths across a local hard drive, often without requiring special permission or alerting the user.

Right now, thousands of employees may be inadvertently violating confidentiality agreements by running consumer AI agents on personal laptops that house their employers’ IP. If settings allow model training from this data, courts may eventually find these trade secrets to have lost legal protection due to dissemination outside the company.

Standard IT audits won’t catch AI data theft

This recent case serves as a warning for how attorneys and founders must approach trade secret investigations. Traditional digital discovery is no longer sufficient because AI tools make it effortless to disperse, alter and recreate data across nonobvious folder paths.

Actions that previously seemed like overkill — such as full forensic imaging of a personal device — are now the bare minimum. Furthermore, AI dramatically reduces the friction of reverse-engineering software and tech products, potentially removing telltale signs that code or data was copied.

Proving theft in AI contexts requires intensive, highly technical expert analysis and carries far more uncertainty than traditional IP litigation.

3 practical steps companies should take

Founders should take three legal and operational steps to proactively protect their business:

  1. Implement strict agentic AI policies: Mandate tight controls and settings that isolate outside AI from company documents. Web-based tools like Claude with strict data privacy policies are vastly safer than open source or desktop apps that crawl local drives. Some AI agents should not be permitted to run at all within an environment containing trade secrets.
  2. Eliminate remote access from unmanaged devices: Shift to a closed cloud environment where data can be viewed and manipulated on a secure server, but files cannot be downloaded locally to a personal desktop. Removing local file downloads eliminates the risk of desktop AI agents indexing proprietary data.
  3. Rewrite your Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements for the AI era: Standard confidentiality agreements need explicit clauses addressing AI use, model training inputs, and a precise definition of data misappropriation through machine learning.

If you suspect an employee has walked away with data or misused it in an AI tool, your first step should be immediate: cut off all system access and retain counsel. Don’t wait until you start losing clients or experiencing financial losses. Feeding trade secrets into AI presents an existential threat from day one.

AI gives individuals the unprecedented ability to compete in spaces where they lack experience, making proprietary data more vulnerable than ever. Modernizing security, policy and legal strategies to address today’s AI threats will help startups and established companies avoid catastrophic exposure.

Seth Kugler is a partner at Grellas Shah LLP , where he focuses on complex commercial litigation, including disputes related to trade secret and IP misappropriation, corporate governance and breach of fiduciary duties, breach of contract, and other complex business disputes. He specializes in preventing and resolving all manner of disputes among and between corporate founders, directors, officers and shareholders, LLC members, and other current and former business partners.

item.title: 5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Robot Training, Space Lasers And Greener Cement
item.description:
This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here .

From teaching robots to do everyday household chores to using lasers to track satellites in space, this month’s crop of interesting startup deals spans some decidedly different corners of tech.

Other startups that caught our eye are working on making cement production less polluting, turning agricultural waste into a useful tool for carbon removal, and helping independent video game developers get their product in front of more players. Let’s take a closer look.

$30M to teach robots by watching humans

Before robots can fold laundry, load dishwashers or prepare meals, they need to learn how humans actually do those things. Maxinsights is betting there’s a big business in supplying the training material.

The Santa Clara, California-based startup this week announced a $30 million seed round led by Peak XV Partners , with participation from Tola Capital , South Park Commons , Ince Capital and Alumni Ventures . The company, founded by veterans of the robotics and autonomous vehicle industries, is building what it calls the data layer for physical AI.

Its approach is surprisingly low-tech in some respects: Pay people to wear cameras while they go about everyday tasks, from washing dishes to preparing food or cleaning hotel rooms. But turning all that footage into something useful for robotics models is more complicated. Maxinsights develops its own recording hardware and AI-powered software to collect, label and organize the data so robots can learn from it.

The startup says it has already captured more than 2 million hours of human activity, with 1.5 million hours ready for use in AI training. Its customers include robotics model developers Genesis AI and Dyna Robotics . It is also developing a sensor-equipped glove called MaxGlove that can capture information cameras can’t see, such as grip strength and the force needed to manipulate objects.

The funding comes amid a massive boom in physical AI investment. Startups in the sector raised $47.4 billion globally in the first half of 2026 , nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, Crunchbase data shows.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026

£8.2M to track satellites with lasers

Space is getting crowded, and keeping track of everything flying around up there is becoming an increasingly complicated problem.

With that in mind, London-based Foundational emerged from stealth this month with £8.2 million (around $11 million) in pre-seed funding led by Inflection , with participation from investors including Type One Ventures , Final Frontier, Backed VC and Adjacent .

The company uses a technique called satellite laser ranging, which involves firing laser pulses from ground stations toward reflectors mounted on satellites. The company says that by measuring how long the light takes to return, its system can calculate satellite positions with millimeter-level accuracy.

While the technology has existed for decades, Foundational is working to make it cheaper and more scalable. Its system combines automated ground stations, satellite-mounted hardware and a software platform called Origin that provides positioning data to satellite operators. The company says its stations cost roughly 30x less than legacy systems.

The technology could prove increasingly valuable as thousands more satellites enter orbit, raising the risk of collisions with other spacecraft and debris. The European Space Agency estimates that around 1.5 million pieces of space debris measuring between 1 and 10 centimeters are orbiting Earth — large enough to cause serious damage to functioning satellites.

Foundational’s raise comes amid a record-setting year for space technology funding. Investors had already poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally by late August , Crunchbase data shows, easily surpassing previous annual records with several months still left in the year.

Related Crunchbase query: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding

$10M to make cement without so much carbon

Cement is the glue holding much of the modern world together. It’s also responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions , per an MIT estimate.

Calgary, Canada-based Cura Climate wants to change that. The startup last month said it raised $10 million in new funding led by Zacua Ventures , with participation from Sandpiper Ventures , Amplify Capital and Vantage Futures , to advance technology that could substantially reduce emissions from cement production.

Cement manufacturing traditionally requires heating limestone to extremely high temperatures, a process that releases significant amounts of carbon dioxide. Cura is developing an electrochemical alternative that uses electricity to separate carbon dioxide from limestone before it enters the kiln.

The company says its process could cut cement-related emissions by up to 85% while also reducing energy consumption. Crucially, the technology is designed to integrate with existing cement plants rather than requiring manufacturers to replace their entire production facilities.

The fresh capital will help fund a pilot plant in Alberta capable of producing 100 metric tons of material annually, as well as engineering work for a larger commercial demonstration facility with a planned capacity of 30,000 metric tons per year.

Cura is among a growing crop of startups targeting industrial processes that have proven particularly difficult to decarbonize. While venture funding for cleantech has fallen well below the peaks of 2021 and 2022, the sector has shown signs of stabilizing. Investors put $15 billion into cleantech-, EV- and sustainability-related startups in the first half of 2026 , with second-quarter investment reaching its highest level since 2024, Crunchbase data shows.

Startups like Cura working on cleaner cement technologies , in particular, have also seen investor interest in recent years.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Cleantech Startup Funding In 2026

$10M to help mobile games find their players

Making a successful mobile game is one thing. Getting enough people to discover and play it is an entirely different — and often very expensive — challenge.

Cyprus-based Mika Games is tackling that problem with an unusual investment model. The company, founded by Wargaming co-founder Nick Katselapov , said this week that it had raised $10 million in new funding led by Flint Capital to help early-stage gaming studios turn promising titles into commercial successes.

Mika isn’t a traditional game developer. Instead, it invests in small studios and helps finance the expensive marketing campaigns needed to attract players.

The problem is something of a catch-22 for developers: They often need hundreds of thousands of dollars in advertising to prove that their games can attract and retain paying users. But the financing providers that fund those campaigns typically want several months of marketing performance data before they’ll provide capital.

Mika aims to bridge that gap by combining equity investments in game development with separate financing for early marketing campaigns. If those efforts demonstrate that a game can acquire players profitably, the studio may then qualify for larger financing arrangements.

The company says it now has five studios in its portfolio, including the developer of Legendale, a farming adventure game with more than 3 million players, and Punko, a tower defense game with more than 500,000 downloads.

The investment comes as gaming startup funding is showing signs of recovery. Companies in the sector had raised around $2 billion globally in 2026 as of late September , already exceeding the full-year 2025 total, Crunchbase data shows.

Mika isn’t the only investor experimenting with alternative financing for game developers. Griffin Gaming Partners earlier this year announced a $100 million fund offering indie studios financing in exchange for a share of game revenue, another sign that investors see opportunities beyond conventional equity funding in the gaming industry.

Related Crunchbase query: Gaming-Related Startup Funding, 2026

$3M to turn coffee waste into carbon removal

Not that you need another reason to look forward to your steaming morning cup of coffee, but consider this: The leftovers from that daily ritual might eventually help remove carbon from the atmosphere.

Zurich-based Cotierra said late last month that it had raised $3 million in funding co-led by PINC, the venture arm of food and beverage company Paulig , and Carbon Removal Partners . Cotierra says it’s developing technology that turns agricultural waste into biochar, a charcoal-like material that can store carbon for long periods while improving soil health.

Biochar itself isn’t new. What’s interesting about Cotierra’s approach is where and how it wants to make it. Rather than transporting bulky crop residues to large centralized facilities, the startup says it’s developing smaller, decentralized reactors that can be deployed close to where agricultural waste is generated. Its technology combines the reactors with software to monitor production, track the resulting carbon removal, and verify the environmental benefits.

The company has initially focused on Colombia’s coffee-growing regions, including Huila, the Coffee Triangle, Antioquia and Santander, where growers face increasing pressure to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. Cotierra says its technology has already been tested on coffee farms and is now moving toward larger commercial deployments, with plans to expand into cocoa, cotton and citrus production.

It’s a potentially appealing business model for both farmers and food companies: Turn an otherwise low-value waste product into something that can improve soil conditions while also generating measurable carbon removal.

Its raise, however, comes against a difficult backdrop for agricultural technology investment. Global funding to agriculture and farming startups remains far below its 2021 peak, when companies in the sector raised $10.5 billion, according to a Crunchbase News analysis earlier this year . Funding to the sector totaled just $2.8 billion through the third quarter of 2026, down even from the $3.5 billion raised in the same period last year.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Agriculture And Farming Funding In 2026

item.title: Exclusive: Slingshot Raises $27M In Seed Funding To Build An Insurer For Those Small Policies Sold At Checkout
item.description:
Slingshot Insurance, an AI-native embedded insurance startup, is emerging from stealth with $27 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.

Rally Ventures and Skyward Group co-led the round, with participation from insurance industry veterans including Jim Hays , who will join Slingshot’s board. Rally is also a co-founder of the Minneapolis-based startup, as part of the firm’s broader approach. So far, it has co-founded roughly eight portfolio companies that have either launched or remain in stealth.

Slingshot, which is led by first-time founder and CEO Ethan Genteman, focuses on small insurance policies that consumers can buy as part of another purchase, such as coverage when booking a flight. Known as embedded insurance, the model puts coverage in front of customers when they might need it.

The startup’s software helps businesses offer those policies by connecting them with insurers that back the coverage. It uses AI to process and share data between the two sides, aiming to reduce the administrative work that can make inexpensive policies costly to offer.

Its first customer and design partner is Vertical Insure , which serves more than 750,000 customers at an average premium of $25, according to Slingshot. Genteman told Crunchbase News that Slingshot’s first program will launch this month.

For now, Slingshot earns revenue as a technology provider working with outside insurers. But the six-person company, which formally began operating July 1, is also pursuing an acquisition that would allow it to back policies itself.

“We’re not a carrier yet, but we are rapidly closing on our carrier,” Genteman said in an interview.

Making the math work on a $25 policy

One product Slingshot is working on would let parents buy insurance when signing a child up for youth sports, Genteman said. A parent spending $2,000 on a volleyball league, for example, might be offered a $25 policy covering cancellation or an injury during the season.

Each policy includes paperwork and coordination with an insurer, and can bring potential claims. But when policies cost so little, managing them can quickly eat into the money they bring in, noted Genteman.

He believes that as vertical SaaS companies increasingly look beyond traditional subscription fees for growth, embedded insurance is “a largely untapped opportunity” to generate incremental revenue from transactions already happening on their platforms while delivering additional value to customers.

“The challenge is that the insurance and regulatory landscape is incredibly complex, and most SaaS companies don’t have the expertise, industry relationships or understanding of where to begin,” he said.

Slingshot aims to solve this by providing a white-glove service for those vertical SaaS companies, helping them go from an insurance product idea to “a fully operational offering.”

He offered a hypothetical example: A program collecting $500,000 in premiums with a 10% margin would have just $50,000 in margin.

“That’s not a viable program for the way incumbent carriers have set themselves up operationally,” he said.

Slingshot’s goal is to replace the spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems used to manage that work with software that connects policy distributors and insurers directly. The company says its AI automates data-heavy tasks while keeping a record of decisions that the businesses involved can review and check.

It charges a 5% technology fee to administer programs through its platform. Acquiring an insurer would let it provide both the software and the financial backing, according to Genteman.

A customer helped shape the business

The difficulties facing Slingshot’s first customer helped bring the startup together.

Rally had already helped start Vertical Insure, which uses software platforms to sell insurance to its customers. According to Genteman, that business had opportunities to introduce more products but struggled to find insurers whose technology and processes could keep up.

“We can design the products our customers need almost overnight, but the industry is highly regulated, and we need delegated authority just to write and distribute what we’ve built,” Vertical Insure co-founder and CEO Brock Noland said in a statement. “The antiquated approval process on the carrier-side slows everything down.”

Even after finding an insurer willing to back a product, connecting the two companies’ systems could create more delays, Genteman said.

Slingshot was built to address those problems, with Vertical Insure helping shape its product as a design partner. Noland is also a Slingshot co-founder.

The opportunity in vertical SaaS

Genteman sees a broader opening among vertical SaaS companies: businesses that sell software tailored to a particular industry.

As vertical SaaS companies look for ways to grow beyond subscription fees, insurance could give them another avenue to make money from purchases customers already make through their platforms, argues Genteman. They already know their customers and what they’re buying, putting them in a position to offer coverage that fits the purchase.

A babysitting platform, for example, could offer coverage to help parents pay for replacement childcare if a sitter cancels at the last minute. Software used by pet boarding facilities could offer coverage for unexpected vet bills if a pet is injured during a stay. An equipment rental platform could let customers add protection at checkout against accidental damage or theft.

Those are examples of what could be developed, Genteman said. Slingshot aims to help vertical SaaS companies take ideas like those and turn them into insurance they can sell, providing both the software and help navigating the insurance industry and its regulatory requirements.

“Insurance becomes another product that can be offered naturally within the existing customer experience,” he said.

For Justin Kaufenberg , managing director at Rally Ventures, that opportunity is familiar. Before joining Rally, he ran SportsEngine , where insurance sold through its software became a key revenue source.

“That experience gave me firsthand insight into the opportunity for software companies to generate revenue through embedded financial products,” he wrote via email.

Kaufenberg sees similar potential across Rally’s portfolio, where most companies combine AI products with financial services. He said founders increasingly want insurance partners that can help them introduce coverage quickly.

Rally co-founded Slingshot to bring insurance backing, underwriting, reporting, claims handling and distribution together in one business.

“To get the carrier, the reinsurance, the underwriting platform, the data flow engine, the reporting capabilities, the claims handling, the embedded distribution engine, and every other part of the offering from a single vendor is unheard of,” Kaufenberg said.

From insurance executive to founder

Before starting Slingshot, Genteman was chief actuarial officer at publicly traded Palomar Holdings , where he also led data. He joined in 2019 and helped build its actuarial and data team as the company expanded beyond earthquake insurance into other coverage types.

That work led him to explore whether newer technology could reduce the costs of running insurance programs. About a year ago, he began coding and building prototypes in his basement. He started talking with Rally toward the end of 2025 and left Palomar on July 1 to run Slingshot.

item.title: The AI IPO Wave Is The Dot-Com Bubble’s Evil Twin. Anthropic’s Delay Just Proved It.
item.description:
By Anurag Gurtu

When a company delays its IPO to show investors better numbers, that’s a strategy. When the NYC pension fund publicly asks you to delay it over AI safety concerns, your chief rival’s CEO calls his own IPO “ill-advised” and postpones it until at least next year, tech stocks are sliding on open-weight model fears, and your own prospectus warns of “existential risks to humanity” from the product you’re selling, that’s not a strategy.

That’s a market sending you a message.

Anthropic ‘s numbers are extraordinary. Its third-quarter 2026 revenue was reportedly $16.8 billion — up 45% quarter on quarter. That means the company’s annualized revenue run rate is roughly $67 billion.

What the S-1 actually says

Here are the numbers from Anthropic’s leaked prospectus :

  • $4.6 billion: Anthropic’s full-year 2025 revenue.
  • $7.33 billion : What Anthropic spent on compute and infrastructure in 2025 alone — more than its total revenue.
  • $42 billion: Anthropic’s net loss in 2025. The roadshow will immediately explain that $34 billion of it was a noncash accounting charge — an adjustment to the estimated value of financing instruments that could eventually convert into shares.
  • $518 billion: How much Anthropic expects to spend, at least, over the course of a decade on AI infrastructure with six partners, including Google , Microsoft and Amazon , according to the confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters . About 80% of the total is noncancelable or payable regardless of usage.
  • $2 trillion: That’s the IPO valuation Anthropic is still targeting for November, a figure representing 435x its 2025 revenue.

One more number from the S-1 that the roadshow will bury: A quarter of Anthropic’s 2025 revenue came from two unnamed customers.

Three signals the market is sending

The IPO delay is the headline. It isn’t the only signal worth reading.

Signal one: NYC Comptroller Mark Levine. Last week, the supervisor of New York City’s pension funds — which reportedly hold roughly $7 million in Anthropic exposure today, but could hold dramatically more if Anthropic enters the Russell 3000 post-IPO — sent a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urging the company to pause the IPO entirely.

The risks he cited are the same ones Anthropic’s own prospectus flags: increasingly autonomous AI systems that could behave in unexpected ways, create security problems, and in the document’s own language, pose “existential risks to humanity.”

Signal two: Sam Altman delays OpenAI ’s IPO. OpenAI has said it will not go public in 2026. CEO Altman called an IPO at this moment “ill-advised” given AI safety concerns, and while that framing is partly strategic — positioning OpenAI as the more responsible actor — it’s also a real signal when the CEO of the second-most valuable AI company in the world looks at current conditions and decides to wait.

Signal three: The chip selloff. Last week’s $2 trillion chip-stock selloff was driven partly by concern over AI-buildout costs. Gartner ’s forecast helps explain the concern: Through 2030, it sees at most $3.6 trillion in revenue attributable to AI data centers, versus $8.5 trillion needed to cover planned investment, financing costs and a 12% return.

The open-weight problem

Here is the structural argument that no amount of Q3 revenue growth resolves: Anthropic’s $2 trillion valuation requires closed-model AI to maintain a durable pricing premium over open-weight alternatives. That premium is being systematically dismantled.

Open-weight AI is challenging the economics behind closed-model valuations. Enterprise adoption rose from 23% to 67% in 2026, with companies reporting 70%–90% cost savings. DeepSeek R1 offers frontier-level performance on most enterprise benchmarks at 7 cents per million input tokens; independent analysis puts Anthropic’s comparable input and output pricing at roughly 18x and 23x higher, respectively.

DeepSeek’s weights are free to download, allowing enterprises to self-host without a model-provider API contract or per-token billing, while the capability gap with closed models reportedly closes within six months of a frontier release.

Against that backdrop, New Constructs — the research firm that called Anthropic’s proposed offering “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility” — calculated that justifying a $2 trillion valuation would require an immediate 10% after-tax operating margin sustained for a decade, extraordinary revenue growth, and $358 billion in annual after-tax operating profit by 2035.

Why this is worse than 1999

The dot-com bubble had a genuine excuse. Nobody knew what the internet would become. The AI IPO wave of 2026 does not have that excuse.

Worldwide spending on AI is forecast to reach $2.59 trillion in 2026 , up 47% year over year, according to Gartner. Yet a July 2025 MIT NANDA report estimated that 95% of the organizations it examined were getting no return from generative AI. Meanwhile, KPMG said in its own report earlier this year that just 7% of surveyed leaders say they’ve established ROI from AI.

This is the context in which Anthropic is asking investors to pay 435x 2025 revenue for a company with $518 billion in locked infrastructure commitments, 25% revenue concentration in two unnamed clients, and a pricing moat that open-weight models are closing in six-month cycles.

The delay from October to November doesn’t change any of those numbers. It adds one quarter of revenue data.

What actually survives this correction

Here is what no AI IPO roadshow will say out loud: The biggest enterprise AI winners will not necessarily own the most expensive model. They will own the architecture that turns any model into governed, auditable, measurable outcomes — through proprietary enterprise data, domain-specific fine-tuning, multiagent orchestration and controls that make autonomous execution trustworthy.

That value does not depend on keeping model capabilities scarce or securing a $2 trillion valuation. It compounds in production, where customers understand that the model is not the product. The deployment is.

The dot-com crash did not happen because the internet was bad. It happened because the price was wrong. AI investors face the same distinction: Real technology does not automatically justify its valuation. A strong quarter and a one-month delay do not close that gap. November simply gives Anthropic more time to explain the math.

Anurag Gurtu , the co-founder and CEO of Airrived , is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk , Tripwire and Sun Microsystems , and a public company, FireEye . He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification.

item.title: Acquirers Are Snapping Up Boom-Era Startups That Haven’t Raised Funding In Years
item.description:
When a venture-backed startup goes a few years without raising a new round, it’s common to presume its odds of a sizable exit have gone down as well.

But that’s often not the case, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. This year, a number of larger acquisitions of private companies involved startups that haven’t disclosed a new investment for more than four years.

Several of these acquisitions are quite recent — and in some cases, quite large. The standout is Uber ’s purchase earlier this month of ezCater , a platform for catering and workplace meals, for $2.3 billion in cash. The deal comes nearly five years after Boston-based ezCater raised its last reported venture funding round.

That’s not the only one. A number of companies whose names might feature on a playlist of 2021 boom-era unicorns have sold to acquirers in recent months, including one-time highfliers like Airtable , Headspace and Miro . In many cases, companies are selling at valuations which, while not puny, are still far below their former peaks.

Who’s getting acquired

To illustrate the extent to which these aging startups are finding acquirers, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of 15 deals involving well-funded companies that haven’t raised equity funding for four or more years.

Post-peak runway

One big issue for older and middle-aged startups is that valuations hit a cyclical peak in 2021 and early 2022. Many companies that raised during that time had difficulty attracting fresh capital or were reluctant to close new rounds at reduced valuations. Even with the more recent AI boom, little went to this cohort.

Moreover, since the 2021 boom-era rounds were quite large, funded startups commonly had the option to cut operating costs and extend their runways with existing capital. As a result, quite a few companies that haven’t raised rounds in years are still chugging along, managing to survive and even grow without more venture funding.

EzCater is a case in point. In the year prior to its acquisition, the business generated more than $2.5 billion in gross bookings. It had an annual growth rate in the high teens, with average order sizes over $400.

That said, even that revenue and growth rate didn’t secure ezCater much of an acquisition premium from its last funding round. At $2.3 billion, Uber’s purchase price is 53% above the $1.5 billion pre-money valuation the catering startup secured in its last funding round in late 2021.

Acquisitions below peak venture valuation

In many cases, even good-sized acquisitions of well-funded startups are occurring at valuations far below former peaks.

Take Miro, a provider of online collaboration tools that agreed to sell to Bending Spoons last month in a deal valued around $1.36 billion. That’s a huge step down from early 2022, when San Francisco-based Miro closed its last round at a $17.5 billion post-money valuation.

Or consider Bending Spoons’ prior purchase of data and workflow platform Airtable , for $1.28 billion in August. That’s barely over one-tenth the $11 billion valuation Airtable secured in its December 2021 Series F.

Fashion startup Everlane is another that lost its shimmer after securing a 2020 valuation in the hundreds of millions. It sold to fast-fashion leader Shein this spring for $100 million.

In the health and wellness sector, meanwhile, Headspace also saw its valuation plunge. The meditation and mental health app sold to Sword Health in a deal reportedly valued around $300 million. That’s well below its peak post-money valuation of around $2.6 billion.

A good thing?

While startup investors aren’t celebrating acquisitions made far under peak private valuations, they’re not the worst outcome. And for startups themselves, they’re also far from a catastrophic scenario.

Of course, every unicorn investor hopes for high-multiple returns. But for startups that go years without funding, the market seems to be telling us that’s not likely in the cards.

item.title: Your Next Customer Might Be An Agent. Here’s How To Build Your Brand For Both Humans And AI.
item.description:
By Toby Coulthard

You’ve just moved into a new house. It’s unfurnished; the walls are bare. Ten years ago, you might have loaded up Google and started searching for furniture that you like, consulting interior design magazines and looking for offers on retailers’ websites. In 2026, however, there’s an entirely different option at your fingertips. You could take a photo of the empty room, upload the image to an AI agent, share your budget and style, and get a list of furniture that suits your preferences. You could even have the agent purchase on your behalf.

Instead of just selling to one customer base — humans — brands are now selling to two.

This second audience of AI agents makes decisions on different criteria than humans. Often, in fact, AI agents will make purchasing decisions before a human ever sees the product page. There’s a real chance that all the emotive copy marketers have so carefully crafted will get broken down and reconstituted by a machine. Just relying on the human touch isn’t enough anymore.

Leave humans in the equation

A word of caution, though: Marketers shouldn’t forget the human entirely in the rush to prepare for AI agents. It’s easy to get carried away with visions of an entirely agentic future. But at the end of the day, each agent is still catering to a human with their own preferences, and personalization will only get more granular over time. The trick is to optimize for both audiences simultaneously, not just one.

Newer startup founders have the advantage here. Established brands have to retrofit decades of copy, guidelines and approval processes to make themselves agent-ready. New brands, on the other hand, can build in copy and a brand voice that’s legible to humans and agents from the very start.

But what does this look like in practice?

To start, brands should work out a distinct voice — and write it down. In most early-stage companies, the brand voice solely exists in the founder’s head. This might work if the copy’s written by a handful of people who work with the founder, but it doesn’t work well when the writer — or reader — is a machine.

AI tools follow explicit rules and drift without them. I’ve spent years at my startup, Jacquard , working out how to get AI agents to write better content, but it’s only now that we’re seeing agents on the other side of the process too — and that makes the rules matter even more.

What a brand sounds like matters, but what it doesn’t sound like matters just as much. Brands should note words never to use and the claims never to make. Often these instincts don’t get written down; they feel obvious to the team who already know them. But if you take the time to spell them out before you have a team — or a machine — producing your copy, you’ll save yourself from running into issues further down the line.

Verify your brand

Marketers also need to realize that product descriptions aren’t just administrative: they’re now core brand assets. In an agent-mediated world, they may be the most-read brand copy you own, since agents read them when looking for a product to recommend or purchase. If two personalized AI agents look for furniture for two different people, they may surface the same chair for both, but with the description tweaked for each user. The source description needs to carry the brand intact.

Where possible, brands need to test channels for both readers. Email inboxes are the clearest current example of the “second reader.” Both Gmail and Apple now summarize messages before the recipient opens them and offer summaries above the body of the email — which may be read before the email itself.

So before sending, check what the AI summary says your email is about. Does the offer survive? Does it maintain what makes you unique? It’s not time-intensive, and it’s a small habit any marketing team can adopt today with no tooling.

Brands also need to ensure they’re measuring the outcome of their marketing — not just the volume. Marketers who measure the success of their materials only by the amount produced will find their data meaningless as AI makes content production easier and easier. Focus instead on business outcomes, conversions and revenue. These are the metrics that will show if your marketing team is really doing their job.

And finally, don’t lose sight of the human. No one knows how fast AI purchasing will scale. Humans are still predominantly the ones reading copy and making purchasing decisions. Even AI agents, the second audience, cater to their users’ preferences.

New founders and brands are best positioned to take advantage of the transition to a dual-audience economy. Though it’s hard to say exactly how, the retail landscape will look very different in five or 10 years. Building these decisions into your brand now is easy.

Retrofitting them later is expensive.

Toby Coulthard is chief product and growth officer at Jacquard , an AI platform that helps brands generate and optimize bespoke messaging at scale.

item.title: When A Startup Sells, Its Employees’ Equity Plans Can Change Overnight
item.description:
By Ron Honig

Acquisitions are reshaping the technology industry. Venture-backed AI companies acquired 195 AI startups this year through late September , already exceeding the total for all of 2025, Crunchbase data shows.

For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years.

A client whose employer was acquired in an all-cash transaction described to me the atmosphere inside the company during the weeks that followed: Employees repeatedly discussed the deal in office corridors, trying to understand what it meant for their equity awards, their jobs and their future. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs.

The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually.

One acquisition, different outcomes

Employees at the same company can emerge from an acquisition with remarkably different financial outcomes.

Some own vested shares. Others hold restricted stock units, stock options or performance-based awards. Their rights depend on grant agreements, vesting conditions and transaction terms. Even two employees holding RSUs may face different payment schedules or employment requirements.

Depending on the agreements, outstanding awards may be settled in cash, accelerated, converted into replacement awards, or remain subject to future conditions. One employee might receive a substantial payment when the transaction closes. Another may have much of the expected value tied to continued employment.

The announced acquisition price provides a reference point. It rarely tells an individual employee everything they need to know about the money they will receive.

This helps explain the conversations my client described. Colleagues may compare the value of their equity without realizing that their contractual rights differ.

Wealth and employment uncertainty

Technology employees with substantial equity compensation often depend on their employer in several ways.

Their salaries, bonuses, career opportunities and investment portfolios may all be linked to the same company.

An all-cash acquisition can reduce their exposure to its share price once vested shares are converted into cash. Other forms of dependence may continue.

The acquiring company may reorganize teams, change responsibilities or introduce retention arrangements. Employees whose unvested awards remain conditional on employment may face difficult choices about staying.

Someone expecting a large payment can therefore feel financially stronger while becoming less certain about their career.

Before making plans

A major acquisition announcement can change personal ambitions long before the proceeds arrive.

Employees may begin considering early retirement, a new business, a career break or a major family purchase.

Those possibilities are worth exploring. But an announced acquisition may still require regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. The headline value of an equity award may differ substantially from the cash ultimately available to its holder.

Taxes, exercise costs where applicable, outstanding liabilities and payment schedules can all affect the outcome. So can the employee’s financial position outside the company.

A substantial payment might make a career change affordable without providing enough capital to fund permanent retirement. Existing pension savings, household spending and future earning capacity remain important.

In my work with technology executives, I have seen expectations about new wealth reshape personal plans before the underlying numbers have been established.

Employees facing a cash acquisition can begin with three questions: What rights do my specific awards provide? When will the proceeds actually become available? And what choices will the resulting after-tax capital support?

The answers may differ considerably among colleagues.

An exit without an exit decision

Founders who sell their companies often participate directly in negotiating the transaction. Employees holding equity compensation generally have much less influence over its timing.

They may have intended to retain their shares for years, sell gradually or remain employed until additional awards vested. A corporate acquisition can replace those plans with a timetable established by the transaction.

For some employees, the result will be substantial financial flexibility. For others, a significant part of their expected compensation may remain connected to future employment.

The period between announcement and closing can be especially difficult because the financial opportunity is visible while important details remain unresolved.

My client’s description of the office corridors captured that experience. The company had made a decision about its future. Its employees were left to work out what that decision meant for theirs.

The acquisition determines the terms of a corporate transaction. Each employee still has to establish how much financial freedom it creates.

Ron Honig is co-CEO and managing partner of From-Honig Family Office , which works with technology executives, founders and families on integrated wealth planning, equity compensation and major liquidity events. His background includes more than two decades in the technology industry.
